rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idols can neither benefit nor harm, and their harm exceeds their doubtful benefit; seeking refuge in them is foolish, while abandoning God deprives people of their true support.
rows.anchor: are not only unable to cause harm or benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse echoes 22:73: both the impotent gods and their idolaters are evil, like leaders and followers who resemble and outdo one another in wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: the seeker and the sought after are helpless and weak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing those who lose hope and seek other protectors, the passage contrasts them with people who remain faithful and righteous through ease and hardship.
rows.anchor: in comfort and discomfort, conducive and adverse circumtances will adhere to faith and do righteous deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because it contrasts with worship at the edge in 22:11, professing faith here means complete, diligent devotion without hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: those among people who worship God standing at one edge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's power to do whatever He intends rebukes reliance on impotent deities and reassures believers to trust Him through harsh trials.
rows.anchor: God has power over everything and can do whatever He intends

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to the despairing person in the preceding context, not Muhammad; these hypocrites turn to other protectors and think God will not relieve them.
rows.anchor: The opinion of those who regard it to be Muḥammad (sws) is against the context

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stretching a rope to the sky is an idiom for making the final possible effort, as also illustrated by 6:35.
rows.anchor: stretch a rope in the sky is a metaphor that means to execute the last and ultimate measure

rows.speaker: Zuhayr and A‘shā
rows.claim: Classical Arabic poetry by Zuhayr and A‘shā uses the rope-to-sky idiom for a final effort.
rows.anchor: Classical poets like Zuhayr (d. 609 AD) and A‘shā (d. 625 AD) too have used this idiom for the final effort

rows.speaker: Abū Muslim
rows.claim: Abū Muslim takes qataʿa to mean travelling a distance, so the person should stretch a rope skyward and climb it.
rows.anchor: According to Abū Muslim the word

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some interpreters understand the command as stopping divine revelation, challenging those who think God will not help His messenger to prevent revelation from coming.
rows.anchor: Some people say that it means “cause divine revelation to cease.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings of qataʿa as stopping revelation or hanging oneself are linguistically and rhetorically unsuitable; although it can mean travelling, that meaning does not fit this context, where ‘climb’ would suit the rope image.
rows.anchor: he should climb) would have been suitable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In classical Arabic qataʿa conventionally means deciding a matter with determination, as in the Queen of Sheba's statement in 27:32.
rows.anchor: this word is conventionally used to decide a matter with determination

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The despairing person may exhaust every measure, even reaching the heavens, but cannot resolve his distress by abandoning God; only faith quenches human nature's thirst and only remembrance of God fills its inner void.
rows.anchor: the thirst found in human nature cannot be quenched by every fountain; it can only be quenched by the fountain of faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despair of God is a prominent cause of polytheism: people seek another support by nature, but only God is real support, so such efforts fail.
rows.anchor: losing hoping in God is a very prominent factor that leads to polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is the only support in both worlds; reliance on someone thought able to protect a person against God's justice will collapse on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: in the next world too He is the only help and support

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse warns that these clear revelations point back to the preceding proofs of monotheism and refutation of polytheism; an implied clause says receptive people believe while the deprived persist in frivolous dispute, as 22:8 indicates.
rows.anchor: the clear arguments in favour of monotheism and refutation of polytheism mentioned earlier

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's established practice is to guide those who use insight and intellect, while those who become deaf and blind have sealed hearts.
rows.anchor: only they receive God’s guidance who use their insight and intellect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews, Christians, and Sabaeans were already mentioned in 2:62; the Magians began as Zoroastrian monotheists but later adopted fire worship and other polytheistic innovations.
rows.anchor: The Magians were originally the followers of Zoroastrianism and this religion was based on pure monothesim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse extends the preceding debate between believers and idolaters to other Arabian religious groups, especially Jews and Christians who actively sided with the idolaters against Islam; God will judge the dispute.
rows.anchor: the Jews and Nazarenes were openly supporting them at every front

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's decision means the consequences of each side's deeds: believers receive reward for their sacrifices, while idolaters, disbelievers, and their allies face their misdeeds.
rows.anchor: the results of every person’s efforts he is undertaking here will come before him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing assertion that God sees everything reassures believers and warns opponents that He observes both their sacrifices and their rivals' schemes and will judge each accordingly.
rows.anchor: He is observing the sacrifices and feats of valour of the believers and also seeing the pranks and conspiracies of their rivals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers and idolaters are the two primary parties, with other sects secondary; 22:19 therefore treats everyone outside the believers as aligned with the disbelievers whatever religion they claim.
rows.anchor: the real factions are these two: the believers on the one hand and the disbelievers and idolaters on the other

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse uses verbs for Muslims, Jews, and idolaters because they were active contesting forces, while nouns mark less active sects whose sympathies nonetheless lay with the idolaters; verbs convey greater movement and commotion.
rows.anchor: there is a certain amount of stir and commotion found in verbs whereas nouns only serve to be signs of distinction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe's objects testify to monotheism through their instinctive Abrahamic submission to God's commands; even the sun, moon, stars, mountains, and cattle follow His laws.
rows.anchor: every object of this universe in its instinctive nature has an Abrahamic temperament

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun itself, often worshipped as a deity, daily stands, kneels, and prostrates before its Lord; the moon's phases and the stars' appearances likewise attest submission.
rows.anchor: day and night it stands, kneels and prostrates before its Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shadows of mountains, trees, and animals always lie opposite the sun, symbolically showing that the Creator, not the sun, deserves prostration.
rows.anchor: the shadow of everything by its very existence teaches us that it is not the sun which is worthy of prostration but in fact its creator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This proof of monotheism is an insinuation rather than a formal logical argument, so it is appreciated by those who reflect on the universe.
rows.anchor: This argument in favour of monotheism is in the form of an insinuation and hence cannot be grasped by logic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shadows in 13:15 show that even a person who rebels by choice has a shadow that remains naturally submissive to God and refuses the indignity of bowing to another.
rows.anchor: his own shadows by its very existence detests this attitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage in 16:48–49 similarly says that created things and their shadows prostrate, alongside all living beings and God's non-arrogant angels.
rows.anchor: all living beings in the heavens and the earth prostrate to God only and the angels of God too

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike nonintentional creation, many people freely submit to God, while others misuse the honor of free choice and disgrace themselves by rejecting truth.
rows.anchor: many people who out of their free will and intention submit to His directives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the universe serves humans, its objects will not accept being worshipped by them; humans, God's best creatures and vicegerents, abase themselves by worshipping inferior deities.
rows.anchor: they worship deities which are much below their status

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened people merit punishment because they have disgraced themselves and tried to belittle their Lord.
rows.anchor: they disgraced themselves and also tried to belittle their Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human rank depends on conduct: God preserves or elevates it when people meet moral standards, and lets them fall toward what they chose; 4:115 expresses this practice and assures the Prophet that he cannot save them after decisive proof.
rows.anchor: their rank and status are kept intact by God and even increased

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Monotheism is humanity's defining distinction; rejecting it makes people lower than the lowliest creation and out of harmony with the universe, even their own shadows.
rows.anchor: their own shadow is in discord with them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two factions in 22:19 are presented as the detailed outcome of the judgment between the parties announced in 22:17.
rows.anchor: these verses, these details are mentioned

rows.speaker: Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī holds that classical Arabic can refer to two or more groups with either the dual or plural, supported by the plural form akhtaṣamū.
rows.anchor: my mentor Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī is of the opinion that if the groups are two or more than two they can be referred to in the dual as well as in the plural

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although several groups were listed, the author prefers that there were really two sides: all communities opposing monotheism and Islam formed one faction, and Muslims the other.
rows.anchor: in reality only two groups existed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disagreement about the Lord refers to the earlier debate over monotheism and polytheism; despite being People of the Book, they openly joined the idolaters.
rows.anchor: the dispute and argumentation that was going on between these two factions regarding monotheism and polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who disbelieved includes every faction siding with polytheism, since polytheism is disbelief in essence; calling it a lesser evil than disbelief contradicts the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: the reason polytheism is called disbelief is that in its essence polytheism is disbelief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clothing of fire reflects opponents who burned with hatred, anger, and jealousy against truth in worldly life; boiling water melts their insides and skin.
rows.anchor: in this world these people in their enmity against the truth seethed and burnt in the fire of hate, anger and jealousy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about being driven back from any torment means there is no escape from any punishment, even if they seek refuge in another torment.
rows.anchor: there will be no chance for them to escape from any of the torments of Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to taste burning punishment is conveyed by the situation itself; no explicit speech verb is needed, and a coordinated clause is understood as suppressed.
rows.anchor: What is portrayed by the situation is more potent than what is portrayed by the tongue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment mirrors the opponents' deeds: those who rejected the Prophet and companions' efforts to save them now face the destruction they had embraced.
rows.anchor: they became their enemies merely because they had tried to save them from this destruction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing Islam's opponents, the verse turns to those who held firmly to truth amid severe opposition and describes their reward.
rows.anchor: those people is referred to who strongly adhered to the truth in the wake of grave opposition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pearl is coordinated grammatically with bracelets, yielding gold bracelets and pearl necklaces; the silk wording covers all their clothing and bedding.
rows.anchor: in Paradise they will be made to wear bracelets of gold and necklaces of pearl

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being guided to a pure word of gratitude means the believers continually praise God when they see His promises fulfilled, as also described in 39:74 and 35:34–35.
rows.anchor: They will express their gratitude when they would see that all the promises of their Lord had been fulfilled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being guided to the praiseworthy God's way refers to reaching the believers' chosen home; angels guide them there, and the passive voice honors them.
rows.anchor: through a group of angels these people will be guided to the way that will lead them to their place of residence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section on verses 25–37 brings the monotheism–polytheism debate to its climax: Quraysh resisted Islam because it threatened their religious and political leadership as custodians claiming Abraham's legacy.
rows.anchor: The debate of monotheism and polytheism reaches its climax in this section

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh controlled the House's keys and Arabia's religious leadership; Abū Lahab led Banū Hāshim and had seized Makkah's public treasury, so they would not surrender these advantages.
rows.anchor: Abū Lahab was their leader. He had forcibly taken possession of the public treasury of Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh barred Muslims from visiting the House and persecuted them into leaving Makkah; the revealed passage explains Abraham's purpose, the House's sacred rites, and tests Quraysh's claim to his legacy while preparing Muslims for their ritual duties.
rows.anchor: they forcibly kept away the Muslims from visiting the House of God and let loose a wave of terror and oppression on them forcing them to leave Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mu’minūn is the counterpart and supplement of al-Ḥajj: the previous sūrah ends with the community's duty to witness the true religion, and this sūrah begins on the same subject, with its opening and closing verses interlocking.
rows.anchor: perfectly enmesh into one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrahs share themes but differ in style and reasoning: al-Ḥajj announces believers' success and disbelievers' disgrace, while al-Mu’minūn details believers' traits and the certainty of disbelievers' humiliation; temporary trials and respite end when truth triumphs.
rows.anchor: Ultimately, the truth will triumph and evil will be routed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–11 promise believers success and Paradise subject to stated conditions.
rows.anchor: Believers are given glad tidings of success and entry into Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 11–22 establish resurrection through signs in human creation and show that the universe's providence entails certain reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: Resurrection in the hereafter is substantiated through the signs of God’s power and wisdom in the creation of human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 23–50 briefly recount earlier prophets, naming Noah, Moses, Aaron, and Jesus while leaving the middle prophets unnamed.
rows.anchor: By referring to Noah (sws) among the earlier prophets, Moses (sws), Aaron (sws) and Jesus (sws) among the later ones
